cards.heading: Definition
cards.question: What does SLO burn-rate alerting alert on, instead of raw error counts or instantaneous error rates?
cards.answer: The rate at which the error budget is being consumed, evaluated over multiple time windows simultaneously.

cards.heading: Four evaluation attributes
cards.question: What four attributes does the SRE Workbook chapter use to evaluate any alerting strategy?
cards.answer: Precision (fraction of alerts marking significant events), recall (fraction of significant events alerted), detection time, and reset time.

cards.heading: Why naive strategies fail
cards.question: Why do the two naive alerting strategies — alerting on instantaneous error rate, and alerting only when the whole budget is exhausted — each fail?
cards.answer: Instantaneous error rate is noisy (low precision); waiting until the whole budget is gone detects problems far too late.

cards.heading: What burn rate means
cards.question: What does a burn rate of exactly 1 mean, and why does normalizing consumption against the budget matter?
cards.answer: A burn rate of 1 spends exactly the allotted budget over the SLO window; normalizing consumption against the budget lets alert thresholds map directly to time-to-exhaustion, rather than being an arbitrary error-count cutoff.

cards.heading: Multiwindow design
cards.question: Why does mature burn-rate alerting pair a long window with a short window (e.g., one hour and five minutes)?
cards.answer: So alerts fire quickly on genuine spikes via the short window while resetting promptly once the problem clears via the long window; a slower, lower-burn-rate pair is also layered beneath the paging pair for ticket-severity issues.
